# Work Log | June 6, 2024

**Date**: 2024.06.06  
**Weather**: Sunny  
**State of Mind**: Good  

---

## Morning Department Meeting Notes

Just finished the meeting. I want to organize my thoughts while they’re fresh, so I’m jotting them down now.

The process optimization plan Xiao Wang proposed today was genuinely impressive. He suggested introducing an early-warning mechanism in the material provisioning phase by flagging inventory thresholds 72 hours in advance. This would give the procurement department much more breathing room. The logic behind the plan is solid; I looked over his data model, and the attention to detail is thorough.

I publicly voiced my approval but made a point to emphasize one thing—this was a result of team innovation, not the credit of any single individual. I noticed Xiao Wang visibly relax when I said that. He’s been a bit discouraged lately because his promotion was stalled; seeing him rediscover a sense of purpose in his work feels more important than any title change.

## Thoughts on the "Continuous Optimization Committee"

During the meeting, I floated a new idea—establishing an internal "Continuous Optimization Committee." The plan is to invite experts from the IT department every two weeks to share knowledge on system architecture. This would give team members a chance to understand the underlying logic rather than just executing procedures.

To be honest, this idea gradually took shape during this recent project. I used to feel like I had to maintain total control over everything—creating perfect plans and having the team follow them step-by-step. But this time was different. When I truly let go and allowed Xiao Wang and the others to experiment and innovate, the results were actually better. It wasn't because I controlled things more effectively, but because they had the space to think proactively.

This realization has had quite an impact on me.

## Changes in Team Atmosphere

The atmosphere in the conference room was noticeably different today. In the past, everyone seemed tense during meetings, afraid that something might go wrong. Today was different; people were proactively asking questions, adding ideas, and even raising doubts. This level of freedom in discussion is, I believe, a very good sign.

There’s a procurement coordination meeting this afternoon, and I’ve decided to let Xiao Wang chair it. He’s never led a cross-departmental meeting before, but I feel he’s ready. This is another area where I want to change—instead of micromanaging everything, I want to give everyone the opportunity to showcase their abilities.

## Reflections

Sitting here in my office, I’ve been wondering: why was I so obsessed with perfect control in the past?

Perhaps it’s because I grew up in an environment defined by rules and order. My father was an engineer and my mother was a teacher; both were the type of people who did everything by the book. I inherited that trait and perhaps even took it to the extreme. But I understand now that order and flexibility are not opposites. True order should involve giving people full autonomy within a framework.

This project has shown me another possibility. Perhaps the definition of professional achievement isn't necessarily a promotion or moving up the ladder; it can also be about doing better in your current position and helping your team grow. I’m no longer so fixated on waiting for opportunities from above; instead, I care more about how to make this department’s systems more robust.

It’s almost as if I finally understand what Wang Xiaofang has been telling me all along: "Not everything needs to be under total control." She is so flexible while I am so cautious, yet over the years, we’ve managed to keep both our home and work lives in perfect order. I realize now that wasn't because of my "perfect plans," but because we found our respective places.

## Follow-up Plans

- Complete the preliminary proposal document for the "Continuous Optimization Committee" by Friday.
- Follow up on the procurement coordination meeting chaired by Xiao Wang to get feedback on his performance.
- Report this management innovation attempt to my supervisor to see if it can be scaled to other departments.
- Discuss this with Wang Xiaofang this weekend; she’ll likely have some interesting insights.

---

**Today’s Insight**: Perhaps the best management isn't about keeping everything under control, but about ensuring everyone can see their own value.

# Wednesday, April 24, 2024, 11:00 PM

I’ve closed the study door. My son is asleep, and my parents have retired to their room. Wang Xiaofang is in the living room watching financial news. I need to get today’s events down on paper; otherwise, these thoughts will just keep circling in my head.

Xiao Wang came to talk to me around 3:00 PM. He was very tactful, but I caught his drift—"Manager Li, I feel that sometimes the requirements for details are a bit..." He didn't finish the sentence, but I knew what he wanted to say: "micromanaged."

At that moment, I wanted to defend myself. I wanted to tell him that the reason I’m so strict about every step is to guarantee quality and maintain our department's reputation within the group. I wanted to say I was doing it for his own good. But I didn't. I chose to stay silent and then asked, "Could you give me some specifics?"

He gave a few examples: the formatting of the production schedule, the lead time for material stocking, even the wording of quality inspection reports. He said, "Actually, I can handle these details, but I feel like I have to wait for your confirmation every time. It’s a bit... stifling."

What was my reaction then? My first instinct was defensive—I quickly listed all the reasons for my strictness in my head. But as I listened to him, I suddenly felt a flicker of uncertainty.

Am I helping the team maintain high standards, or am I just controlling them?

This question has been stuck in my mind. I pulled out my work logs from the past three months. How many pieces of feedback did I give Xiao Wang? I counted... an average of over ten per week. How many of those were actual errors? Maybe 30%. What about the other 70%? It was just me feeling things "could be done better."

I admit, I like being in control. I like knowing that every step is within my plan. It gives me a sense of security. But what if that security is built on suppressing the team?

Xiao Wang said something later that I keep replaying: "Manager Li, I really want to do better, but sometimes I don't know when it's 'good' and when it's 'not good enough'."

I didn't give him a satisfying answer. I just said, "I'll think about it."

Now I am thinking. Really thinking.

I’ve always viewed my high standards as respect for the work and responsibility toward the team. But maybe... maybe I’ve turned perfectionism into a form of control? Am I using "standards" as an excuse to maintain my grip on everything?

If that’s the case, then how much of the "high efficiency and low error rate" I’ve built in the department over the years is due to a good system, and how much is because the team is being kept on too tight a leash? If I loosen up, would they still perform well?

Or would everything fall into chaos without my strict oversight?

I don't know. That’s what I’m most unsure of right now.

I’m going to talk to Xiao Wang again tomorrow. But this time, it won't be to explain why I’m right; it will be to truly listen. To understand what kind of guidance he needs, rather than what kind of control.

I thought I had this project all figured out. But now I realize that the thing that truly needs to change might not be the project plan, but myself.

— Li Minghui

# Work Log

**Date:** October 13, 2025  
**Recorded by:** Li Minghui  
**Department:** Production Planning Department

---

## Record of Events

### 1. Career Development Talk with Xiao Wang

I had an extensive conversation with Xiao Wang in the office this afternoon. He has been feeling low lately due to limited promotion opportunities, and his work performance has slipped as a result. Having noticed this issue persisting for some time, I took the initiative to speak with him today.

During our talk, I shared some perspectives with him. I explained that professional achievement isn't necessarily defined solely by promotions. Sometimes, going deeper and more granular in one's current role—helping the team optimize processes and improve efficiency—is highly meaningful in its own right. I cited several examples from our department over the past two years, ranging from process streamlining to the piloting of the new software system. These improvements didn't happen because of title changes, but because we were willing to think critically and experiment within our existing framework.

Xiao Wang listened attentively. He later admitted that he had indeed placed too much weight on promotions and now understands that he can make significant contributions from his current position. By the end of our meeting, his attitude had shifted noticeably, and he mentioned he would re-evaluate his approach to his work.

### 2. Work Assessment

This conversation served as a form of validation for me as well. I realized that when I am able to help subordinates reframe their understanding of professional value, my own understanding of the work becomes clearer. This is not just a managerial responsibility; it is a process of mutual growth.

Xiao Wang’s situation reflects potential common issues within the department. I suggest strengthening communication on this topic at the team level moving forward, helping everyone realize that opportunities for optimization and innovation are embedded in their daily tasks.

### 3. Next Steps

- Continue to monitor changes in Xiao Wang’s work status.
- Consider sharing some reflections on career development during departmental meetings.
- Continue pushing forward with the implementation of the new software system, as it provides an excellent opportunity for team growth.

---

**Notes:** This dialogue reminded me that effective management is not just about processes and data; more importantly, it is about understanding and guidance.

Xiaofang, I wanted to talk to you about something.

I had another chat with Mr. Wang yesterday, and this time we went a bit deeper. He said something that I’ve been thinking about ever since: "Stability isn't about staying still; it's about being able to handle change." I used to think I was safe just staying in my current position, but looking back now, that mindset is actually quite dangerous.

Together, we mapped out a three-year plan. It’s not about jumping ship immediately or making any radical moves, but rather:

**Year 1**: Deepen my current professional expertise. I’m already doing well in production planning, but I can go deeper—into things like supply chain optimization and new cost-control methods. At the same time, I’ll start systematically learning new management tools and industry knowledge.

**Year 2**: Take on cross-departmental projects. I want to leverage the trust I’ve built to get involved in some group-level optimization projects and gain broader experience.

**Year 3**: Based on the growth from the first two years, I’ll evaluate internal promotion opportunities—or, if necessary, I’ll have enough leverage to consider other options.

I’ve saved this plan on my phone and broken it down into specific monthly goals. You know how I am—this is the only way I’ll actually follow through.

But I want to hear your thoughts. Does this plan affect our family’s financial planning? Do we need to adjust anything regarding the mortgage or the kids' education fund? I’m not looking to take huge risks, but if I’m going to invest time and energy into learning new things, I might need to adjust how I spend my time at home.

To be honest, I’ve felt a bit different these past two weeks. It’s not anxiety, but... more like anticipation? I feel like I’m no longer stuck in place, but finally taking the initiative.

What do you think?

Xiaofang, I’ve been lying in bed thinking for a long while, and I felt like I needed to tell you this.

I’m still playing that sentence of yours over in my head: "I’ve been waiting for you to say these things." It suddenly hit me that over these past three years, you’ve been watching me—watching how I’ve slowly let go of that "everything must be perfect" mindset. I hadn't realized that until now.

I think I should tell you things more often—not because you need to hear them, but because I need to say them. Your understanding means so much to me. It’s not the "I support whatever you do" kind of understanding; it’s the fact that you see the changes within me, even before I can see them clearly myself.

It’s a strange, wonderful feeling. I used to think I had to have everything under control, including my emotions. But you’ve been there all along, not waiting for me to "succeed" or get a "promotion," but waiting for me to truly accept myself.

Shall we talk more tomorrow? I feel like we need to think about our new plans together. Not the "making a to-do list" kind of thinking, but really sitting down to see what it is we truly want now.

Goodnight.

# WeChat Chat with Mr. Wang

**2024-09-30 18:32**

Hi Mr. Wang, it’s been a while. How have you been?

I’ve been meaning to reach out. Since that last workshop, it feels like something has finally clicked for me. I wonder if you’ve been feeling anything similar.

To be honest, I’ve gone through a pretty interesting shift lately. Before, I was fixated on getting promoted, always feeling like my current position wasn't high enough, like something was missing. But recently, I realized I might have been asking the wrong questions.

Instead of chasing labels like "promotion" or "success," I’ve started asking myself, "What kind of person do I want to be?" It sounds a bit abstract, but it really changes everything.

A while back, my dad’s blood pressure was acting up, so I started talking to his doctors constantly and putting together a health plan for him. That whole process taught me something—there are things we can control and things we can’t. All I can do is give it my best and then accept the parts that are out of my hands. I think that applies to work, too.

I’m still putting everything I’ve got into my current projects, but I’ve also made it clear to myself that I won’t sacrifice time with my kids for a promotion. Ironically, this has made me more efficient because I know exactly where my boundaries are.

What about you? Are you still wrestling with career development stuff? Or have you ever thought that maybe what we need isn't a change in position, but a change in how we view the position?

I have goals now, but I also have patience. I’m looking toward the future, but I’m also cherishing the present. Surprisingly, I feel a lot less stressed.

I’m not sure if any of this helps. Sometimes I feel like people our age are all going through something similar. It’s not about giving up; it’s about finding a more sustainable rhythm.

---

**2024-09-30 18:45**

By the way, if you have some time, let’s catch up. My head feels a lot clearer than before—maybe I can help you sort through some of your thoughts too.

Xiaofang, I just got back from the office and I’m still buzzing a bit. I had the talk with my boss about the career development discussion mechanism, and he agreed to let me run a pilot program within our department first.

To be honest, I was pretty nervous before stepping into his office. I’d prepared so much material, worrying that I might have missed a detail somewhere. But once we sat down to talk, I actually calmed down. Maybe it’s because I’ve thought this idea through so thoroughly that I was able to just lay it out step by step.

The most interesting part was that he didn't ask, "How will this help you get promoted?" and that wasn't on my mind either. We spent the whole time discussing "how to help the younger staff see their career paths more clearly." You know, this feels completely different from when I was gunning for a promotion before. Back then, it was this tense "I need to climb the ladder" feeling; now, I actually feel more grounded.

I told him I’d put my heart into making this pilot work. It’s not about proving anything; I just really want to see if Xiao Wang and the others can find more possibilities through this system. Thinking back to how frustrated Xiao Wang used to be—his whole attitude toward work has changed now. This feeling—seeing someone else change because of your suggestion—is more fulfilling than any expectation of a promotion.

And hey, none of this would have happened without you. You’ve been there all this time, listening to me ramble about my anxieties—from me agonizing over "whether I should keep climbing" to finally realizing "I can actually make this role more meaningful." You didn't give me the answers directly, but your questions—like "Are you really unhappy right now?" and "How did you feel when you were helping Xiao Wang?"—helped me figure it out for myself.

Want to go over the specific pilot plan together tonight? I’d love to hear your thoughts.

Subject: Departmental Production Process System Audit – Invitation to Participate

Dear Colleagues,

Lately, I’ve been reflecting on something: while our department’s ability to maintain high efficiency and low error rates over the years is certainly commendable, does it mean our processes are already optimal? I believe the answer is no.

To address this, I would like to launch a "Departmental Production Process System Audit" project. The core idea is simple—to preserve our existing strengths while proactively identifying areas for improvement. This is not a critique of the status quo, but rather a routine "physical exam." Just as machinery requires regular maintenance, our processes need periodic review.

Specifically, I would like everyone to:
- Identify any steps in your daily workflow that feel clunky, redundant, or overly tedious.
- Propose any suggestions for optimization—no matter how big or small.
- If you have ideas, please send them to me by next Friday, or we can organize a brief discussion session.

I welcome all thoughts and suggestions. This project isn't something for me to complete alone; it’s about us working together to refine our workflows. As those on the front lines, you know best where improvements can be made. I trust your professional judgment.

We expect to complete the preliminary assessment for this project by mid-October. We can discuss the specific next steps as we move forward.

Thank you for your cooperation.

Minghui Li
September 27, 2025

Xiaofang, I’ve been thinking about that moment today.

When you said, "I’ve seen how much you’ve grown," I was a bit stunned. It wasn’t that I didn’t believe you; it was more the sudden realization that these changes weren't just swirling around in my head—they were actually visible to you. Being seen by the person closest to me... it just feels different.

I can’t quite put into words everything that’s happened over these past three months. It started with that workshop, listening to Teacher Liu talk about stability and risk, then those conversations with Mr. Wang. Gradually, I feel like I’ve shifted from someone who always tried to "control everything" to someone who can accept that "some things are just out of my hands." It sounds simple, but once I actually started doing it, the pressure just fell away.

Do you remember how I used to be? My dad’s blood pressure, Haoran’s early education classes, the mortgage, the pension fund—I had to calculate everything down to the last detail, terrified of making a single mistake. I still care about those things, but I’ve learned the wisdom of finding the line between what I can and cannot control. When I take care of my dad now, I still make a detailed health plan for him, but I can also sincerely tell him, "We’ll leave the rest to time." I could never have said that before.

What moves me most is that you’ve been watching all along. I didn’t talk to you much about these thoughts, yet you felt the change in me. You might even know better than I do which direction I’m heading.

I feel like I have both purpose and patience now. I’m looking toward the future, but I’m also starting to cherish the present. When I play blocks with Haoran, I no longer think, "Is this a waste of time?" I actually enjoy the moment. Even when we go over the accounts together, our conversations feel different—it’s no longer about anxiety, but about planning our life together.

I’d really love to sit down and talk with you about what you’ve seen over these three months. Your perspective means a lot to me.

Xiaofang, are you asleep? I wanted to talk to you about something.

When I was chatting with Dad today, he said something that I’ve been thinking about ever since. He said that what matters most isn't how much you do, but who you do it with. I didn't say much at the time, but the thought has been stuck in my head.

I suddenly realized that I’ve been getting bogged down lately. I’m working overtime more and more frequently; I want to spend more time with Haoran on the weekends, but work stuff still ends up creeping into my mind. The time we spend going over the accounts together is also shrinking. Even the time I have for my parents is being squeezed out.

I’m not just venting—I’m just thinking that maybe we need to recalibrate. It’s not that work isn't important, it’s just… how do I put this? It feels like I’ve been using "getting things done" as a substitute for "being with the people who matter." Those two things aren't the same.

You’ve always said I’m too stubborn, too obsessed with making everything perfect. I’m starting to understand what you mean now. Maybe a perfect plan isn't as important as having a sensible direction and then actually having the time to be with family.

What do you think? For instance, are there adjustments I could make at work, or how should we reallocate our time on the weekends? I’d love to hear your thoughts, because you always see the things I miss.

February 20, 2023 – Past 10:00 PM

My conversation with Xiao Wang today keeps playing over in my head.

He mentioned that his promotion prospects look bleak and that he’s thinking of moving on. As I listened, I suddenly found myself saying things I don’t usually say—that a promotion isn't the only metric of success, and that one can find value even in their current role. After the words left my mouth, I was a bit stunned. It sounded like I was advising him, but in reality, I was trying to convince myself.

He later asked if I had been thinking about these things too. I said yes, that I’m learning to "accept the status quo." When that phrase came out of my mouth, it felt foreign. Acceptance? Me?

I’ve always been the type of person who needs to have everything under control. Folders on my desk are color-coded, household accounts are tracked to the last cent, and even my child’s future is planned out well in advance. But recent events have made me wonder: what exactly is this control protecting?

My father’s blood pressure hit 155. That number felt like a sudden warning. I’ve looked up piles of information, made a medication schedule, and have been pestering Dr. Zhang with questions. But honestly, no amount of planning or data can change the core reality. All I can do is be there when he measures his pressure, remind him to take his pills, and then... accept the fact that he is getting older.

It sounds pessimistic, but it’s actually not. While talking to Xiao Wang, I suddenly realized that accepting the status quo is actually a mature choice. It’s not about giving up; it’s about doing what you can while acknowledging reality.

I’ve done a good job at work. The department’s efficiency and error rates—the data speaks for itself. Promotion opportunities might be limited, but that doesn't mean my work is valueless. Maybe I should stop waiting for that higher position and instead go deeper into what I’m doing now.

Things at home have become more complex. My parents are here, Haoran is still young, and Xiaofang is swamped with work. There is never enough time. I used to see this as a problem to be solved, but now... I don’t know. Maybe this is just what life looks like. Imperfect, but real.

This last thought is a bit messy, but I want to write it down anyway: I’ve always treated stability as the ultimate goal. Choosing a state-owned enterprise, choosing to climb steadily within a system, even choosing to settle down in one place. But does stability really exist? Or is my understanding of it too narrow?

Perhaps stability isn't about things staying the same, but about maintaining your balance amidst the changes.

More tomorrow.

# Memo: Conversation with Father & Follow-up Actions

**Date**: November 22, 2025 (Evening)  
**Location**: Living Room  
**Participants**: Father, Minghui Li  

---

## Key Takeaways

**Father’s Current Status**
- Blood Pressure: Stable ✓ (Monitored by Dr. Zhang; medication is effective)
- Mental State: Much better; no longer constantly worrying about his health.
- Real Needs: **Not medical data, but companionship and shared activities.**

**Key Discovery**
While chatting with my father today, I realized I’ve been asking too many "medical questions"—blood pressure readings, dosages, and dietary restrictions. What he actually wanted to say was that he wants more time to do things with us, rather than being treated like a "patient in need of care."

When I shifted the conversation and asked, "Is there anything you’ve been wanting to do lately?" his eyes visibly lit up. He mentioned wanting to build LEGOs with Haoran and going for walks in the park with me on weekends.

**Reflection**
I have been trying to manage uncertainty through "control"—obsessing over medical details and drafting health plans. But some things are simply beyond my control. Instead of getting bogged down in the details, I should focus my energy on "being there." That is what my father truly needs.

---

## Personal Notes

This conversation made me realize something: I’ve been striving to "keep everything under control," but so much of life is inherently unpredictable. My father’s health will fluctuate, my child’s growth will bring surprises, and work will always have its variables.

Instead of letting this uncertainty haunt me, I need to learn to "strive for excellence where I can exert control, and practice acceptance where I cannot." For my father, the best form of health management isn't my constant research or reminders; it’s making him feel the companionship and trust of his family.

Wang Xiaofang was right: "You don't need to solve everything. Sometimes, just being there is the best solution."

I used to wonder: Why has the issue of promotion been bothering me so much? Later, I realized the problem wasn't the position itself, but that I treated the position as my sole marker of achievement.

My current understanding is this:
- **Position-Centric Mindset**: Value = Job Level. Promotion equals success; no promotion equals stagnation. In this case, once you hit a ceiling, you get stuck.
- **Competency-Centric Mindset**: Value = Ability to solve problems, create value, and help others grow. A position is just a vessel for competency, not the competency itself.

This shift actually happened to me. My sense of fulfillment no longer comes from "being a manager," but from "being able to improve departmental efficiency through systematic methods" or "helping young employees like Xiao Wang find a new career direction."

**Format of the Sharing Session**

  2. The turning point (workshops, conversation with Mr. Wang, my wife’s advice)

## Risk Assessment & Mitigation

This needs to be handled with care. I don’t want people to feel like I’m "lecturing" or "preaching," nor do I want this to become an extra burden.

**Potential Risks**:
- Some might think this is just an excuse for "hopeless promotion prospects" → I need to emphasize that this isn't passive self-consolation, but a well-thought-out transformation.
- Some might see it as "chicken soup for the soul" (empty platitudes) → I need to use specific data and cases to show how this framework guides my actual work.
- The sharing might trigger career anxiety in some → I need to be prepared to listen rather than trying to "fix" their problems.

**Mitigation Measures**:
- Make it clear from the start: This is my personal experience, not a standard answer. Everyone’s situation is different.
- Prepare 3-4 concrete cases (real situations within the department) instead of vague theories.
- If someone raises a concern, my role is to "accompany their thinking" rather than "provide the answer."
- Follow up individually with interested colleagues after the meeting.

How will I know if this sharing was effective?

1. **Minimum Expectation**: 2-3 colleagues proactively approach me after the meeting to discuss their career development ideas.
2. **Moderate Expectation**: Everyone seriously considers the difference between "position" and "competency" during the discussion.
3. **Ideal Expectation**: Someone changes their perspective on their own career dilemma because of this session and starts trying a new direction.

## Core Realization

Some things don't need to be perfect; they just need to be functional.

This sentence has been playing on loop in my head lately. Yesterday, while talking to Xiaofang about those minor home repairs, she laughed and said I was overthinking it. I realized then that I’ve been applying production-line standards to every detail of my life—and that, in itself, is the problem.

---

## Distinguishing the Three Levels

**Where to strive for excellence (Controllable + High Impact):**
- Production scheduling and quality control at work
- My son’s educational planning and the quality of our time together
- Family financial planning and long-term reserves

**Where functional solutions suffice (Controllable + Low Impact):**
- Daily chores and home maintenance
- Administrative tasks
- Scheduling

**Where to practice acceptance (Uncontrollable):**
- My father’s health
- The timing of career promotions
- The uncertainties of a child’s growth

I used to put everything into the first category. I see now that the cost of doing so is simply too high.

---

## A Recent Example

The faucet was leaking, so I gave Master Wang a list of over ten technical details. He said, "I can handle all of this, don't overthink it." At the time, I thought he was being unprofessional; now, I realize he was right.

A functional faucet and a perfectly installed faucet improve life to roughly the same degree. However, the energy I invested in the latter was ten times greater.

This shift in perspective has made me feel lighter. Truly.

---

## Implications for Work

After talking with Xiao Wang, I’ve been reflecting. Perhaps I should adjust my approach to departmental management as well—not by lowering standards, but by allocating energy more intelligently. Save perfectionism for where it truly matters, and use standardized processes for everything else.

Efficiency doesn't necessarily come from perfection; sometimes it comes from the decision that "good enough is enough."

---

## Reminders to Self

Apply this principle the next time I encounter these situations:
- When bogged down by details → Ask if this truly requires perfection.
- When feeling exhausted → Check if I’m over-refining low-impact tasks.
- When friction arises with family → It might just be my perfectionism acting up.

Life doesn't need to be perfect; it just needs to be meaningful.

# Collective vs. Individual Decision-Making

**Date: December 8, 2023, 9:30 PM**

An idea has been swirling in my head lately, and it became much clearer after discussing the financial plan with Xiaofang today. I need to get this down.

## The Root of the Problem

I used to think that doing things well meant I had to figure everything out, decide everything, and execute everything myself. Office files had to be categorized my way, household accounts organized by my logic, and even the kids' education plans had to be fully drafted by me before I’d even ask for input.

But what was the cost? I was exhausted. Not physically, but mentally. Because I was carrying the weight of every decision and ruminating on every single risk.

## The Recent Shift

During those two weeks at the workshop, a case study shared by Teacher Liu made me realize something: **What I perceived as "control" was actually "isolation."**

A truly good decision isn't about me being the most thorough thinker; it’s about us thinking together and complementing one another.

Xiaofang comes from a finance background, and her perspective is entirely different from mine. I look for "risk minimization," while she looks for "yield maximization." I used to think she was being too risky, but now I understand—her "risks" are actually opportunities I failed to see.

## Tangible Changes

**At Home:**
For this latest financial plan, I didn't just hand her a finished product. We built it together from the start. She came up with three ideas I hadn't considered, two of which were objectively better. When I told her, "This isn't just my plan; it's ours," she smiled and said it was the most comforting thing she’d heard from me in years.

**With My Father:**
Regarding his recent blood pressure issues, my initial instinct was to research everything, talk to the doctors, and decide on a medication regimen myself. But when he asked me, "Are you being a bit too tense?" I realized—he’s an adult with his own judgment. I should be helping him understand the situation, not deciding for him. Now, we go to check-ups together and listen to the doctor’s advice as a team. He asks for my thoughts, and it’s actually brought us closer.

**In the Department:**
The situation with Xiao Wang gave me a lot to think about. Since his promotion prospects were slim, I sat down with him—not to tell him "what to do," but to ask, "What other possibilities do you see?" He came up with ways to optimize his current role on his own. It made me realize that delegation should work the same way. It’s not about me setting rules for them to follow; it’s about discussing the optimal process together.

## Why This Works Better

1.  **More Information:** A single perspective always has blind spots. My wife’s flexibility, my father’s experience, and my subordinates’ front-line feedback are all things I can’t see on my own.
2.  **Stronger Execution:** When people participate in a decision, they buy into it. They aren't just passively executing; they are actively driving it forward.
3.  **Lower Risk:** It sounds counterintuitive, but it’s true. Multiple people assessing risk is more thorough than one person doing it alone. My caution + Xiaofang’s flexibility + my father’s experience is a much safer combination than me acting in a vacuum.
4.  **Less Guilt:** This is the most important one. I used to stay late at the office and bring work stress home, being mentally absent even when playing with the kids. Now that I’ve handed more decision-making power to my team, they’ve started thinking proactively, which allows me to be truly present with my family.

## Next Steps

*   In Monday’s department meeting, try delegating some of the production scheduling decisions to Xiao Wang and the team.
*   Work with Xiaofang to turn the new financial plan into a dynamic spreadsheet that we review together regularly, rather than me maintaining it alone.
*   Keep talking to my father about his thoughts, especially regarding his retirement plans—he’s surely been thinking about it for years, and I need to listen.

## Final Thoughts

"Stability" isn't about things remaining "unchanged," nor is it about "me maintaining tight control." True stability is finding balance amidst change. And that balance requires the collective wisdom of others.

I understand now why some people seem both stable and flexible—it’s because they aren't fighting the battle alone.

I used another example—like a house that needs regular inspections and minor repairs to stay in good condition, rather than waiting for a major disaster to force a massive renovation.

# Internal Memo

**Date:** April 28, 2025 (Afternoon)
**Subject:** The "Mentorship Function" within the Managerial Role — Thoughts on an Integrated Framework

---

## I. The Core Question

A recent conversation with Xiao Wang made me realize something: I am currently acting as both the Production Planning Manager and a sort of "career mentor." Can these two identities truly merge? Or am I just deceiving myself—using the narrative of "helping others grow" as an excuse for stagnating in my current position?

I need to think this through clearly.

## II. Defining "Helping Others Grow"

It cannot remain a vague concept. What exactly did I do during my conversation with Xiao Wang?

1.  **Listened to his predicament** — He expressed frustration over a perceived lack of promotion prospects.
2.  **Shared my own transformation** — I told him how I used to be obsessed with promotions, only to realize later that the goal itself might have been flawed.
3.  **Redefined "achievement"** — Using my own experience, I explained that professional success can mean "doing your current job better" rather than just "climbing to a higher position."
4.  **Empowered him with choice** — I didn’t tell him what he "should" do; I asked him what he "wants" now.

These were real interactions. But does this constitute my "mentorship" function?

The key is: **This isn't extra work; it’s part of management.** A good manager should naturally help subordinates understand their professional value, not just assign tasks.

## III. Possibilities of Integration — and the Risks

**Possibilities:**
*   I am already doing it. The conversation with Xiao Wang happened naturally; it wasn't a pre-designed "mentorship program."
*   These dialogues can boost employee satisfaction and loyalty, which in turn improves departmental stability.
*   I am gaining a deep sense of fulfillment I’ve never felt before—and it’s not disingenuous.

**Risks:**
*   Will this be seen as "overstepping"? As a manager, my primary duties remain production scheduling and quality control. If I pour too much energy into the "mentor" role, will my core responsibilities suffer?
*   Is this satisfaction from "helping others grow" a tool for self-deception—making me more complacent and less inclined to fight for my own promotions?
*   If I propose a "career development discussion" mechanism to my superiors, will I be seen as acting outside my authority?

## IV. Relationship with Existing Responsibilities

To clarify: These two identities **are not in conflict; they are mutually reinforcing.**

*   As a manager, my duty is to ensure the efficiency of production plan execution.
*   As a "mentor," I help subordinates understand their value and growth opportunities within that process.
*   An employee who feels seen, understood, and valued will perform better.
*   In turn, better results provide the subordinate with a genuine sense of achievement.

These are not two parallel lines, but two sides of the same coin.

## V. Future Action Plan

**Short-term (This month):**
*   Maintain regular informal talks with Xiao Wang, but don't overdo it. Observe if this relationship is actually helping him.
*   Consciously bring up the topic of "career development" in department meetings to gauge the reactions of other subordinates.
*   Record key insights from these conversations to build a foundation for further reflection.

**Mid-term (3 months):**
*   Draft a framework for "career development discussions"—it doesn't have to be formal, but it must be clear.
*   Consider proposing a pilot mechanism to my superiors. However, I must provide a solid justification: How does this help improve departmental performance?

**Long-term:**
*   If this direction is approved, gradually institutionalize it.
*   If not, I will at least continue to practice this philosophy in my daily work.

## VI. A New Definition of "Professional Achievement" — Confirmed Version

I am now certain:

**Promotion is no longer my ultimate goal.** This isn't a compromise; it’s a genuine shift in perspective.

What I care about now is:
*   Can I do a better job in the Production Planning Department?
*   Can I help my subordinates understand their professional value?
*   Can I create more tangible value for the company?

The answers to these questions fulfill me more than the question of "Can I become the General Manager?"

## VII. Final Self-Reflection

If I am still in this position ten years from now, will I regret it?

...

No. Not if, during those ten years, I have:
*   Optimized the department's processes to their absolute limit;
*   Helped a dozen subordinates find their professional direction;
*   Raised my child alongside Wang Xiaofang;
*   Looked after my parents' health.

A life like that is worth living.

August 16, 2025 – Evening

It wasn't until I saw Haoran at the park today that I realized I might have been doing something incredibly stupid all along.

I took him to the park this afternoon and, as usual, sat on the bench, poised to spring into action at any moment—to catch him if he fell, to intervene if he clashed with other kids, to stop him from putting something dirty in his mouth. But he didn't even glance my way. He ran straight toward a group of kids by the sandbox, squatted down, and started building. It was that simple.

I sat there watching him for nearly twenty minutes. He didn't need me at all. In fact, it felt like I was the one who was redundant.

That thought stung a little.

It suddenly hit me: lately, I’ve been so anxious about whether he’s struggling to adjust to preschool, or if he needs more of my time and protection. I even discussed taking some time off work with Xiaofang just to be home with him. But watching him play happily with that little girl in the red dress, I finally understood—the problem isn't him.

The problem is me.

I’ve been trying to control a two-year-old’s growth with a "perfect plan." It’s like managing a production schedule at work; I want to map out every step and eliminate every risk in advance. But a child isn't a manufacturing process. He has his own rhythm, and he’s much tougher than I gave him credit for.

Sitting on that bench, for the first time, I consciously chose to do nothing. I didn't lean in, I didn't warn him to be careful, and I didn't interrupt his play. I just watched. It felt foreign, a bit unsettling, but at the same time, there was an indescribable sense of relief.

Maybe this is exactly what I’ve been missing lately.

I’m constantly thinking about how to do better, how to avoid mistakes, and how to keep everything under control. Work, family, my son’s education, my father’s health... I try to foresee every possible problem in every single area. The result is that I’m exhausted, and I’m likely putting invisible pressure on Haoran in the process.

Maybe I need to learn to let go. Not to give up, but to let go.

When I shared this with Xiaofang tonight, she just smiled and said, "I’ve been wanting to tell you that for a long time." Her reaction left me a bit speechless, but also grateful. At least someone is watching over me, even when I can’t see myself clearly.

I don't know what tomorrow will bring, but after this afternoon, I feel like I’ve finally seen things in a different light.

I’ve been fixated on the idea of a promotion, feeling like I might have hit a ceiling in my current role. But perhaps the issue isn't about whether to "jump" to the next level, but rather how I can make more meaningful adjustments within my current position.

---

## Current Status Check

**What’s working well:**
- Departmental efficiency and quality control are consistently stable—that’s a fact.
- The team has strong execution capabilities, and our processes are highly standardized.
- These are solid achievements that shouldn't be overlooked.

**Where I feel stuck:**
- A perceived lack of new challenges.
- Uncertainty about what else I can contribute.
- Waiting for a promotion that might be an indefinite wait.

---

## A New Approach

**It’s not a binary choice between "promotion" or "giving up."**

Instead, it’s about making meaningful attempts based on my current foundation:

1.  **Cross-departmental Collaboration** — There is still room to optimize the interface between Production Planning and other departments. Could I lead a process integration project?
2.  **Talent Development** — A recent conversation with Xiao Wang made me realize I could be more systematic about career mentoring for my subordinates. This helps them and provides a new challenge for me.

4.  **Internal Certification or Further Study** — It doesn’t have to be a master’s degree, but I could pursue deeper learning in project management or data analysis.

---

## Mindset Adjustment

**Key point: This isn't a compromise; it’s a more conscious choice.**

- I don’t need a massive change to prove my worth.
- Small adjustments, if headed in the right direction, can also lead to growth.
- Stability does not equal stagnation; it’s about finding balance within change.

The benefits of this mindset:
- It reduces the anxiety that "everything I have now isn't enough."
- It allows me to focus on doing the work in front of me well.
- If a new opportunity does arise, I’ll be ready for it.

---

- [ ] Schedule a brief check-in with my supervisor—not to push for a promotion, but to understand the future direction of the department.
- [ ] Continue communicating with younger employees like Xiao Wang, and lean into this "mentor" role more intentionally.

---

Perhaps I’ve been asking "Where else can I go?" when the more important question is "What more can I contribute from where I am now?"

The former makes me anxious; the latter brings me peace.

- **What is the worst-case scenario?** List it out specifically.
- **What is the probability of this worst-case scenario?** Let the data speak.
- **If it actually happens, can we handle it?** Is there a Plan B?
- **What is the cost of inaction?** Sometimes, staying the course is the greater risk.

This framework allows me to weigh options rationally rather than retreating the moment I think, "This is too risky."

### Uncontrollable Domains → Learn to Accept

**Father’s Aging**

- He has his own rhythm; I cannot live his life for him
- My role is companionship and care; I must leave the rest to time

**Conflicts Between Work and Family**
- Overtime is sometimes necessary; I cannot eliminate this conflict entirely
- But I can control the frequency and quality—work less overtime, and when I do, keep my family in my heart

# Personal Memo | A Framework for "Control" vs. "Acceptance"

**Date**: October 12, 2024  
**Author**: Li Minghui  
**Subject**: A Practical Checklist for Life Philosophy

---

## Foreword
A few recent conversations with my father have finally made something clear to me. I used to try to manage and plan every single detail, but that only ended up exhausting me and everyone around me. I realize now that some things deserve my perfectionist energy, some only require practical solutions, and others are simply beyond my control—and those, I must learn to accept.

I’m writing this framework down to clear my head and to serve as a quick reference for whenever I face similar dilemmas in the future.

---

## I. The Controllable Sphere (Strive for Excellence)

**At Work**:
- Precision in production scheduling → Continue to optimize; this is my expertise.
- Standardization of departmental processes → Worth the time investment.
- Clarity of communication with subordinates → This directly impacts execution.

**At Home**:
- Weekly financial reviews with my wife → Maintain the rhythm.
- Quality of time spent with my son (even if quantity is limited) → Be present; no distractions.
- Reminders for my father’s medication and scheduling his check-ups → These are things I can do.

**Personal**:
- My own sleep schedule and routine → Maintain.
- Habits of learning and reflection → Continue.
- Attention to detail during home repairs → This gives me a sense of satisfaction.

---

## II. The Uncontrollable Sphere (Sincere Acceptance)

**My Father’s Health**:
- The natural aging process → Accept.
- The progression of his hypertension (fluctuations may occur even with medication) → Accept.
- His moods and mindset → I can offer companionship, but I cannot change them.

**My Son’s Growth**:
- His natural talents and interests → Not something I can fully design.
- His performance in preschool or extracurriculars → There are too many factors I can't see.
- The person he eventually becomes → I can guide, but I cannot control.

**Career Development**:
- Corporate personnel restructuring → Out of my hands.
- Decisions made by upper management → I can do my job well, but promotions aren't entirely up to me.
- Macro shifts in the industry → I can adapt, but I cannot change them.

**Life’s Hiccups**:
- Minor issues around the house → Just fix them; they don't need to be perfect.
- Matters involving relatives and friends → Help where I can; accept it when I can’t.

---

## III. Differences in Attitude

| Sphere | Attitude | Action | Mental State |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Controllable** | Strive for Excellence | Set standards, check regularly, optimize continuously | Proactive, responsible, pursuing excellence |
| **Uncontrollable** | Sincere Acceptance | Do what is possible, then let go of the rest | Calm, patient, empathetic |

---

## IV. Recent Practical Examples

**The Loose Bathroom Tiles**:
- **Old Me**: Would have planned a full bathroom renovation and listed every potential problem.
- **New Me**: Patched the loose tiles and told Xiaofang, "If more issues come up later, we’ll deal with them then."
- **The Shift**: Precise handling of the controllable + acceptance of the uncontrollable.

**My Father’s Blood Pressure**:
- **What I can control**: Reminding him to take his meds, encouraging moderate exercise, keeping him in good spirits, and regular monitoring.
- **What I can’t control**: How his body responds to these measures; the process of aging.
- **My attitude**: Do my best with the former; stop feeling anxious about the latter.

**Preschool Classes**:
- **What I can control**: Choosing the right classes, punctual drop-offs/pick-ups, playing with him at home.
- **What I can’t control**: Exactly what he absorbs in class, his learning pace, whether he "wins the rat race."
- **My attitude**: Do my part and enjoy the process of growing together.

---

## V. Reminders to Myself

1. **Don’t mistake "acceptance" for "giving up"**  
   Accepting what is uncontrollable doesn't mean I don't care. I will still do the parts I can.

2. **Review this list periodically**  
   Over time, some things may move from "uncontrollable" to "controllable," or vice versa. Stay flexible.

3. **Keep communicating with Xiaofang and my parents**  
   This framework shouldn't be built in a vacuum; I need to listen to their perspectives.

4. **Apply this at work too**  
   Don't feel like everything must be under control just because I’m a manager. Give subordinates space and be patient with uncertainty.

---

## VI. Final Thoughts

At 38, the most important thing isn't managing everything to perfection, but finding my own rhythm. Striving for excellence where I have control, and practicing sincere acceptance where I don't—this way, I won't lose my commitment to quality, nor will I be weighed down by perfectionism.

This framework makes me feel much lighter. It’s not about avoidance; it’s about a wiser allocation of attention.

---

*Remember to bring this framework to mind the next time I’m fixing the house or spending time with my son.*

## New Principles (Trial Phase)

### 1. Presence Over Instruction
- My role is to be a **companion**, not a drill sergeant.
- The goal isn't for him to do it my way, but for him to know that "we can figure this out together."
- This builds **trust** rather than **dependency**.

### 2. Ask, Don’t Tell
- When he struggles with the blocks, don't jump in with "it should go like this."
- Instead, ask: "What do you think will happen if we put it this way?" or "Are there any other ways to try?"
- Let him discover the solution himself rather than passively receiving answers.

### 3. Observe, Don’t Correct
- Don't be in such a rush to point out every "mistake."
- First, observe what he is thinking and understand his logic.
- Sometimes his "mistakes" are actually just a different form of exploration.

### 4. Build a "We" Mentality, Not "I’m Teaching You"
- Replace "You should..." with "Let's try..."
- Replace "Let me tell you..." with "I'm not sure either, let's see together."
- This makes him feel **respected** rather than corrected.

---

## Reflection
This shift is really about my own growth. I used to think that being "responsible" meant arranging everything perfectly and teaching him every detail. I realize now that **presence itself is the best form of teaching**.

Xiaofang is right—I need to let go of the obsession with "perfect instruction" and simply experience the process of being with him.

I’ve realized that I’m not actually afraid of change itself; I’m afraid of forced, unprepared change. But if I’m the one planning it, preparing for it, and controlling the pace, it feels completely different.

# Work Log - February 11, 2025

**Project Name:** Production Scheduling Optimization Pilot Program
**Recorded by:** Li Minghui
**Date:** 2025-02-11
**Meeting Time:** 2025-02-10 14:00-16:30

---

## Meeting Overview

An expanded departmental meeting was held this afternoon to discuss three improvement proposals for the production scheduling system. This meeting was a bit different—I changed my usual moderation style and actively invited team members to raise doubts and suggestions, rather than simply presenting decisions as I had in the past.

The results were unexpectedly positive.

---

## Summary of the Three Improvement Proposals

### Option 1: Scheduling Adjustments Based on Predictive Maintenance
- **Core Logic:** Reserve equipment maintenance windows during scheduling to reduce unexpected downtime.
- **Risk Assessment:** Low risk. Requires coordination with the equipment department for maintenance data, but the process is clear.
- **Implementation Cycle:** 2-week pilot; data accumulation to be completed by mid-March.
- **Expected Outcome:** 8-12% reduction in scheduling delay rates.

### Option 2: Linkage Mechanism Between Material Inventory and Scheduling
- **Core Logic:** Adjust scheduling based on inventory cycles to avoid material backlogs or shortages.
- **Risk Assessment:** Medium risk. Requires establishing real-time data interfaces with the procurement department, involving system modifications.
- **Implementation Cycle:** 4 weeks of development; pilot in May.
- **Expected Outcome:** 15% increase in material turnover rate and improved scheduling stability.

### Option 3: Rapid Iteration Mechanism for Quality Feedback
- **Core Logic:** Issues identified during quality inspections are immediately fed back into the scheduling system to automatically adjust subsequent batches.
- **Risk Assessment:** Medium-to-high risk. Requires redefining process permissions and decision-making rules, which may impact existing approval chains.
- **Implementation Cycle:** 6 weeks of design; pilot in June.
- **Expected Outcome:** 20% reduction in rework rates, though the impact on scheduling stability needs close monitoring.

---

## Key Shift

At the start of the meeting, I followed my usual routine by outlining the frameworks of the three options. Halfway through, however, I stopped and asked everyone: "What problems do you see with these plans? Does anyone have a better idea?"

There was silence for about 10 seconds. Then Xiao Wang raised his hand.

He made a very interesting suggestion: **Establish a "buffer layer" between Option 1 and Option 2—using dynamic inventory to absorb the uncertainty of predictive maintenance, rather than letting the schedule take the direct hit.** He even drew a simple flowchart; the logic was very clear.

My first instinct was to judge the idea on the spot. But I caught myself. I realized that my role right now isn't "decision-maker," but "listener." So, I carefully recorded his suggestion, asked a few follow-up questions, and invited him to join the project team to help flesh out the idea.

Seeing this reaction, several other colleagues began offering their own thoughts. Someone mentioned difficulties in coordinating with suppliers; another pointed out technical hurdles with system interfaces. These were all things I hadn't fully considered before.

**This is important.** I realize now that my past "efficiency" may have been built on "ignoring dissenting opinions." That approach allows for quick decisions, but it leaves too much behind.

---

## Personal Reflection

This meeting gave me a deeper understanding of something: **Stability isn't about standing still; it's about continuous optimization within a controllable range.**

I told the team: "Our processes are good, but we must regularly check for areas of improvement. Improvement isn't about overturning everything; it's about making the system more resilient while maintaining core stability."

As I said this, I realized I wasn't just talking about workflows—I was talking about my own philosophy of life.

In the past, I feared change because change meant risk. But now I understand that **the greatest risk is an unwillingness to change.** Without change, a system ages. Without optimization, a process becomes rigid.

This realization started at the financial planning workshop, and now I am bringing it into my work.

---

## Follow-up Actions

1. **By this Friday:** Work with Xiao Wang to complete the detailed design of the "buffer layer" proposal.
2. **Next Monday:** Communicate with the Procurement, Equipment, and Quality Control departments respectively to confirm the feasibility of each plan.
3. **By the end of February:** Finalize the priorities and timeline for the pilot programs.
4. **Mid-March:** Launch the pilot for Option 1 and establish a data monitoring mechanism.

---

## Data Records

- **Meeting Attendance:** 12 people (including core department members).
- **Number of participants who offered suggestions:** 6 (a significant change from the usual average of 1-2).
- **New suggestions:** 1 major proposal (Xiao Wang’s buffer layer plan).
- **Meeting Duration:** 2.5 hours (1 hour longer than planned, but much more productive).

---

## Final Thoughts

I wonder: if I had moderated meetings this way from the beginning, would I have discovered these issues much sooner?

But there’s no point in dwelling on that. What matters is that I’ve realized it now. Furthermore, I believe this "listening" approach will not only improve my work but also make the team feel valued. Xiao Wang approached me after the meeting and said he was happy to be invited to participate in the project. That kind of sentiment doesn't show up in data reports.

When I got home tonight, I mentioned this to Wang Xiaofang. She smiled and said, "It seems you’ve really changed." I asked her what she meant, and she said, "Before, you were always so certain of your decisions. Now, you’re willing to listen to others."

I thought about it, and she’s right.

The discussion framework was designed as follows:
1. Review specific work achievements over the past 12 months (let the data speak).
2. Analyze the competency accumulation behind these achievements.
3. Compare against job requirements to identify gaps and strengths.
4. Formulate the direction for the next stage of development.

---

## II. Discussion Process and Key Shifts

**2:10 PM - Diagnosis**

Xiao Wang started with the same old rhetoric: "There are no new positions in the department; no matter how hard I work, I won't get promoted." Instead of refuting him directly, I asked: "How did that production scheduling system optimization project you led last year turn out in the end?"

He was taken aback for a moment, then said: "It was alright. The scheduling accuracy improved from 88% to 94%."

**2:15 PM - Data Review**

I pulled out a spreadsheet—data on department members' work that I track regularly. I pointed out:
- The three projects he participated in, each with quantified results.
- The reduction in rework rates (from 6.2% to 3.8%) he achieved through quality control process improvements.
- The two new hires he mentored, and their current levels of independence and accuracy.

As Xiao Wang looked at the data, his expression began to change. He said, "I didn't realize I had done so much..."

**2:25 PM - Competency Mapping**

This was the pivotal moment. I asked him: "If we reverse-engineer these results, in which areas do you think you’ve made the most significant progress?"

He began listing them himself: problem analysis, project coordination, and mentoring. I added: "These are actually the core competencies required after a promotion. Look at it from another perspective: you aren't 'waiting for a promotion'; you are 'preparing for one.' And based on the data, you’re already doing a great job."

**2:35 PM - Path Confirmation**

Together, we mapped out his next steps:
- Continue deepening project management skills by aiming to lead a cross-departmental optimization project independently.
- Systematically summarize his work methodologies into reproducible process documentation.
- Conduct a progress check-in with me every month.

**Xiao Wang’s Shift:**
- Emotion: From "disappointed" to "focused."
- Perception: From "passive waiting" to "proactive building."

- ✓ Used data rather than "chicken soup" for the soul; much more persuasive.

# Memo on Family Education Plan - Developing Haoran’s Adaptability

**Date**: Sunday, February 16, 2025, 15:30  
**Subject**: Cultivating resilience and adaptability through designed failure experiences  
**Status**: Draft – To be finalized after discussion with Xiaofang

---

## Core Philosophy

While playing blocks with Haoran recently, an idea struck me: instead of always helping him build the perfect structure, I should consciously let him experience "failure" within a safe environment. Not actual failure, but learning how to face situations where things don't go as planned and finding ways to rebuild on his own.

This concept stems from my recent reflections—I’ve realized that my greatest takeaway from these past years isn't that I got everything right, but that I learned how to stay calm amidst change and find direction within uncertainty. If we can plant this seed in Haoran’s subconscious while he’s young, it might be more valuable than any early childhood education class.

## Specific Methods

**Scenario Design Principles**:
- Conducted in a completely safe environment.
- Consequences of failure are controllable (e.g., blocks falling, unfinished builds).
- I observe from the side without immediate intervention.
- Give him ample time and space to react, adjust, and retry.

**Actionable Activities**:

1. **Block Building Games**
   - Build a relatively complex structure together.
   - When it’s nearly finished, I "accidentally" knock part of it over.
   - Observe his initial reaction: Crying? Giving up? Or trying to fix it?
   - Provide varying levels of encouragement or guidance based on his response.

2. **Puzzles / Construction Toys**
   - Choose tasks that are challenging but achievable for him.
   - Intentionally leave some "incorrect" connections.
   - Let him discover the problem himself and attempt to adjust.

3. **Small "Accidents" During Outdoor Activities**
   - Playing in the sand or building things at the park.
   - Don't clear obstacles in advance; let him encounter minor setbacks during exploration.
   - For example, if a spot he wants to climb is a bit high, let him figure out a way up.

## Observation Metrics

We need to record his behavioral patterns in these situations:

- **Initial Reaction Time**: How long does it take for him to react after the failure occurs (rather than just staring blankly)?
- **Emotional Expression**: Does he cry or throw a tantrum? How long does it last?
- **Recovery Speed**: How long does it take to move from frustration to being willing to try again?
- **Problem-Solving Approach**: How does he try to fix it or restart—does he mimic my methods or come up with something new?
- **Willingness to Retry**: Does he proactively ask to try again, or does he need encouragement?

This data is crucial as it will reveal Haoran’s "adaptability rhythm."

## Implementation Plan

**Frequency**: At least one conscious "design" per week; one full observation record per month.

**Timing**: Weekends are best, as he is usually in a good mood and I won't be distracted by work stress.

**Recording Method**: 
- Simple notes are enough (date, activity, his reaction, my observations).
- Keep it low-friction; the key is identifying trends over time.

**Coordination with Xiaofang**: 
I need to discuss this idea with her. She might worry about Haoran feeling discouraged, but I want her to understand: we aren't creating problems; we are teaching him how to face them. We must ensure the home atmosphere remains supportive, not critical.

## Further Reflections

The long-term goal of this plan isn't to make Haoran someone who is "unafraid of failure"—that would be unhealthy. Rather, it’s to help him understand that:
- Changes in plans are normal.
- Failure is not the end.
- Starting over is always possible.
- Sometimes the best solution is to adjust the old plan rather than tearing it all down.

Come to think of it, this reflects my own recent understanding of work and life. I used to think "stability" meant things staying the same; now I realize "stability" is actually maintaining your rhythm amidst change. If I can pass this understanding on to Haoran, it will be well worth the effort.

---

- [ ] Try it once with Haoran this weekend
- [ ] Record observations from the first session
- [ ] Discuss the idea with Xiaofang
- [ ] Adjust the plan based on feedback

# Work Schedule Optimization Plan - Pilot Version

## Core Concept

Once Haoran starts kindergarten in September, our daily schedule at home will shift significantly. With my parents spending less time childcare, Xiaofang and I will have a bit more flexibility. ---

## Detailed Proposal

**Monday - Thursday (Concentrated Phase)**
- Primary coordination and decision-making for production scheduling.
- Focused handling of quality issues.
- Communication with upstream departments and material verification.
- Data consolidation and weekly report preparation.
- **Goal**: Compress critical tasks into these four days to ensure maximum efficiency and quality.

**Friday (Flexible Phase)**
- Address leftover issues and unexpected contingencies.
- Prepare contingency plans for the following week.
- Internal department training or knowledge sharing.
- If no urgent matters arise: early clock-out or focus on long-term planning.
- **Goal**: Maintain emergency response capabilities without being consumed by daily minutiae.

---

## Potential Advantages

- ✓ Potential boost in departmental efficiency (focusing resources on priorities).
- ✓ More autonomy on Fridays for family time or personal errands.
- ✓ A clearer work rhythm, allowing subordinates to better plan their own tasks.
- ✓ Aligns with the new family dynamic once Haoran starts kindergarten.

---

## Points to Validate

- ? Can Fridays truly remain flexible, or will they be disrupted by ad-hoc tasks?
- ? Will this arrangement impact the department’s emergency response capacity?
- ? Will upper management perceive this as a decrease in work commitment?
- ? Will the workload from Monday to Thursday become overwhelming in practice?

---

## Prerequisites & Communication Plan

**To-Do List:**
1. Discuss the idea with Xiaofang first → Get her feedback, especially regarding the Friday flexibility.
2. Run a two-week trial within the department → Observe actual results and gather feedback from subordinates.
3. Prepare for communication with leadership → Emphasize that this is "workflow optimization," not "reduced input."
4. Adjust departmental workflows → Ensure coordination mechanisms are seamless for the Mon-Thu period.

**Communication Angles:**
- **To Superiors**: This is an experiment to improve departmental efficiency and output quality.
- **To Subordinates**: The new rhythm provides more clarity for their own planning.
- **To Family**: This isn't about avoiding work, but about working more effectively.

---

## Potential Risks & Mitigation

| Risk | Mitigation Measure |
|------|--------------------|
| Sudden pile-up of work on Friday | Reserve at least 2 hours of "buffer time" for emergencies. |
| Skepticism from leadership | Prepare a data-driven efficiency comparison. |
| Subordinates struggling to adapt | Maintain open communication during the trial and adjust promptly. |
| Excessive pressure Mon-Thu | Set reasonable workload caps and implement in phases. |

---

## Next Steps

- [ ] Discuss with Xiaofang this weekend (bring it up during Sunday night's budget review).
- [ ] Start the departmental trial next Monday.
- [ ] Evaluate results after two weeks and prepare to brief leadership.
- [ ] Refine the plan based on feedback.

---

## Core Framework: Shifting from "Role-Centric" to "Competency-Centric"

I had a conversation with Haoran last night while playing with building blocks that I felt was worth recording. He wanted to build the entire castle in one go and started getting frustrated halfway through. I told him: "Look, sometimes we don't need to finish the whole goal at once. We can build a solid foundation first, then add layers one by one. If every layer is stable, the whole castle will stand firm."

He took it to heart and started breaking down the task—bottom layer first, then the middle. He was so happy every time he finished a level.

**This scene is a microcosm of my own shift over the past few months.**

Before, I was constantly thinking about "how to get promoted to a higher position," much like Haoran trying to finish the castle in one breath. But now I realize—what truly matters isn't the final job title, but doing the work solidly at your current level.

Competence speaks for itself. When you streamline processes, manage a team efficiently, and control costs effectively in your current role, those skills become your greatest assets. A title is merely the external validation of those capabilities.

---

## Key Talking Points for Departmental Sharing

1. **"The role is the result; competence is the cause."**  
   Promotions usually happen because you’ve already proven yourself in your current role. Instead of waiting for a title change, focus on solidifying your capabilities first.

2. **"Doing the work in front of you is more important than chasing distant goals."**  
   This isn't about giving up on goals; it’s about breaking them down into actionable stages. By putting your heart into each stage, the long-term results will be far better.

3. **"Systemic thinking is more valuable than isolated breakthroughs."**  
   Our department is recognized not because of one superstar, but because our processes, systems, and teamwork are standardized. This systemic value is the hardest thing to replace.

---

## Applicability Analysis by Career Stage

| Career Stage | Core Dilemma | How the Framework Applies |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **New Employees** | Eager for quick promotion; prone to short-termism. | Emphasize the importance of "building a stable foundation." Current accumulation is the basis for future growth. |
| **Mid-level Staff** | Hitting a ceiling; feeling stagnant. | This is exactly where I am. The focus shifts from "waiting for opportunities" to "creating value." The title stays the same, but the scope of influence expands. |
| **New Managers** | Struggling to define their new role. | A manager's value isn't in the title, but in their ability to help the team grow. This is a shift in competence, not just status. |

---

## Pre-meeting Checklist

- [ ] Ensure the framework doesn't sound "preachy" (Keep the tone peer-to-peer; use "my experience" rather than "you should").
- [ ] Prepare 2-3 specific cases: Haoran’s building blocks, the department’s efficiency gains, Xiao Wang’s career transition.
- [ ] Anticipate pushback: Someone might ask, "But promotion spots are limited"—be ready with an answer.
- [ ] Time control: 8 mins for the framework, 3 mins for cases, leave room for discussion.

---

## Personal Reflection

This shift is real for me. It’s not "chicken soup for the soul"; it’s something I am actually living through.

Working more overtime means less time with Haoran, which makes me feel guilty sometimes. But through this process, I’ve realized that "whether every task is truly meaningful" matters more than "how much I did."

Improving departmental efficiency, standardizing team management, and helping young employees like Xiao Wang find their career path—the value of these things doesn't change whether my title is "Manager" or "Director."

Perhaps the true meaning of this sharing session isn't what I say, but whether we can redefine "career success" together.

## Background

Around 2:00 PM, Xiao Wang took the initiative to come see me. I’ve been keeping an eye on his performance lately—he’s still diligent, but there’s a noticeable dip in his morale. Today, he laid it all out: he failed the promotion assessment again, and he’s starting to doubt whether he’s hit a ceiling in this role.

I’ve heard this narrative many times. There are quite a few young employees in the department like him, all agonizing over the question: "Why am I still just a supervisor?"

## The Conversation

Instead of falling back on the usual routine of "encouragement" or "analyzing promotion criteria," I asked him a question: **"What do you think is the difference between doing a job well and making something happen?"**

He was taken aback. I continued by sharing that I’ve been reflecting on my own work recently and realized something—I used to treat promotion as the only goal, as if moving up was the only definition of success. But I see now that sometimes, if you can drive real innovation and make a genuine contribution in your current position, the sense of fulfillment is no less than that of a promotion.

I gave him an example. Some of the most valuable improvements to our department’s production processes over the years actually came from ideas proposed by junior colleagues. They didn't get promoted for it, but they changed the efficiency of the entire workflow. That has inherent meaning.

## Core Perspective Shared

The gist of what I told him was this:

> "Career development takes many forms. Progress doesn't always have to mean a promotion. Sometimes, innovating and contributing more within your current role can bring even greater satisfaction. You’re a supervisor now—so think about what else you can do in this position that no one else has done. Thinking this way actually takes the pressure off."

He asked me, "So, does that mean you don't want to be promoted anymore?"

I replied, "No. I’m not ruling out the possibility. But I no longer treat it as my sole objective. If the opportunity arises, I’ll go for it. But if it doesn't, I won't let that negate the value of what I’m doing now."

## Xiao Wang’s Reaction

He fell silent for a while after hearing that. Then he said he needed to go back and give it some thought. This reaction was calmer than I expected. He didn't suddenly become overjoyed, but he stopped ruminating. To me, that felt more authentic.

Before leaving, he said, "Manager Li, hearing you say that made me realize that our department's material management system actually has room for optimization. I’d thought about it before, but I figured it wasn't within my scope of responsibility, so I didn't pursue it."

That was exactly what I wanted to hear.

## Management Insights

This conversation made me reflect on my own management style. In the past, I was mostly "directing"—telling subordinates what they should do. Now I’ve found that sometimes sharing my own thought process can be more effective at sparking their initiative.

I wasn't teaching him "how to get promoted"; I was helping him redefine "what success means." It’s a subtle shift, but the effect seems different.

Young people like Xiao Wang aren't anxious because they lack effort; they’re anxious because they’ve pinned all their expectations on a single goal. If I can help them see a diversity of possibilities, they become more relaxed and better able to realize their potential.

## Follow-up

I will continue to observe Xiao Wang’s state. If he actually starts innovating on the material management system, then this talk will have had a practical impact. Regardless of whether a promotion happens, that kind of contribution is valuable in its own right.

This also serves as a reminder to me that as a manager, my responsibility isn't just to manage processes, but to help team members find their own rhythm and sense of purpose.
